questions.stem: Which article do French nouns ending in « -tion » usually take, like nation, question, solution (all English-lookalikes)?
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in « -tion » take « la » — la nation, la question, la solution — and it covers hundreds of words that look like their English cousins. Roughly half of French nouns announce their gender in the ending, which is the closest thing to a shortcut the language offers.

questions.stem: Which article do French nouns ending in « -té » usually take, like beauté (beauty), santé (health), difficulté (difficulty)?
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in « -té » take « la » — la beauté, la santé, la difficulté — and it usually turns an adjective into a noun. Roughly half of French nouns announce their gender in the ending, which is the closest thing to a shortcut the language offers.

questions.stem: Which article do French nouns ending in « -ette » usually take, like baguette (stick loaf), fourchette (fork), serviette (napkin)?
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in « -ette » take « la » — la baguette, la fourchette, la serviette — and it often marks a smaller version of something. Roughly half of French nouns announce their gender in the ending, which is the closest thing to a shortcut the language offers.

questions.stem: Which article do French nouns ending in « -ance » usually take, like chance (luck), distance (distance), connaissance (knowledge)?
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in « -ance » take « la » — la chance, la distance, la connaissance — with no exceptions worth learning. Roughly half of French nouns announce their gender in the ending, which is the closest thing to a shortcut the language offers.

questions.stem: Which article do French nouns ending in « -ure » usually take, like voiture (car), nature (nature), peinture (painting)?
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in « -ure » take « la » — la voiture, la nature, la peinture — with very few exceptions. Roughly half of French nouns announce their gender in the ending, which is the closest thing to a shortcut the language offers.

questions.stem: Which article do French nouns ending in « -ment » usually take, like moment (moment), gouvernement (government), monument (monument)?
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in « -ment » take « le » — le moment, le gouvernement, le monument — and it is one of the most reliable masculine endings. Roughly half of French nouns announce their gender in the ending, which is the closest thing to a shortcut the language offers.

questions.stem: Which article do French nouns ending in « -eau » usually take, like bureau (desk), gâteau (cake), chapeau (hat)?
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in « -eau » take « le » — le bureau, le gâteau, le chapeau — with „l'eau“ as the exception everyone meets first. Roughly half of French nouns announce their gender in the ending, which is the closest thing to a shortcut the language offers.

questions.stem: Which article do French nouns ending in « -isme » usually take, like tourisme (tourism), racisme (racism), cyclisme (cycling)?
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in « -isme » take « le » — le tourisme, le racisme, le cyclisme — and these words are usually recognisable from English. Roughly half of French nouns announce their gender in the ending, which is the closest thing to a shortcut the language offers.

questions.stem: Most nouns ending in « -age » are masculine. Which of these is feminine?
questions.explanation: „La plage“, „la page“, „la cage“ and „l'image“ are the -age exceptions, and they are common enough to be worth memorising as a short list.

questions.stem: Why does « l'hôtel » not show its gender?
options: Hotels have no gender in French
„L'“ is a third article for borrowed words
„Le“ shortens to „l'“ before a silent h, hiding the article
questions.explanation: French elides „le“ and „la“ to „l'“ before a vowel or silent h, so the article stops telling you the gender. You have to find it another way — „un hôtel“ shows it is masculine.

questions.stem: Which article do the days of the week take in French?
questions.explanation: Days, months and seasons are masculine: le lundi, le printemps. „Le lundi“ with the article also means 'on Mondays', habitually — the article is doing two jobs.

questions.stem: In « une voiture rouge », why is the adjective after the noun?
options: Colours are always placed last in a sentence
Most French adjectives follow the noun
questions.explanation: Most French adjectives follow. A small group comes first — beau, nouveau, grand, petit, jeune, vieux, bon, mauvais — and those are the exceptions worth memorising rather than the rule.

questions.stem: What happens to « le » and « la » in the plural?
questions.explanation: „Les“ covers both genders, which makes the plural the one place French gender stops mattering for the article — though the adjective still has to agree.
